notes:
I couldn't cover everything you asked for. I ran out of searches before I could check any Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), the NET Bible notes or bibleodyssey.org. Where the notes below show older Catholic or Greek readings, they come from what the Protestant commentaries say about the Latin Vulgate, the Greek Septuagint (LXX) and Gregory the Great. Guzik's Enduring Word page and the Pulpit Commentary page were both cut off when I loaded them, after verses 12 and 19. So my notes on verses 20 and 23 are thin.

**Key sources:** Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/ · Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html · Matthew Henry: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_018.cfm

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: cutting yourself off from family and community usually shows selfishness. God made us to live in community, like his own triune nature. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Pulpit: a hard verse. The KJV reads it as praise for setting yourself apart to pursue wisdom, as Aben Ezra did, but Pulpit says the Hebrew doesn't really allow that. Most scholars read it as a criticism of the conceited man who goes his own way. The LXX and Vulgate read a different Hebrew word ("occasion" instead of "desire"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html
- Henry gives both readings. One is a rebuke to people who are proud of standing apart and advancing new notions of their own. The other is the KJV's call to work hard at seeking wisdom. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_018.cfm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the fool only asks questions to show how clever he is. His folly comes from focusing on himself instead of God. Waltke notes the Hebrew verb elsewhere describes drunken Noah uncovering himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Pulpit: the fool's only pleasure is showing what's in his heart. Teaching him is like casting pearls before swine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**v. 3**
- Henry sees two meanings. Wicked people treat others with contempt, and they also bring shame on themselves and their families. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_018.cfm
- Pulpit: the contempt is the sinner's own growing scorn for everything good. It quotes Gregory the Great on sin as a well with no bottom. Both the Septuagint and the Vulgate make the wicked man the victim instead of the actor, and Pulpit says the Hebrew doesn't support that. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the point isn't that all speech is deep, but that we reveal the depths of our heart by the words of our mouth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Pulpit: "man" here means the ideal wise man, whose words can't be measured or used up. The LXX reads "heart" instead of "mouth." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik lists reasons people favour the wicked: misplaced compassion, wanting to please, bribes. He quotes Bridges: the case, not the person, must be heard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Pulpit: "accepting the person" means judging by appearance, wealth or family. Jude and other New Testament writers use the same Greek idiom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: arguing is the fool's nature and invites correction. Bridges notes Paul's list of human sin in Romans 3:13–14 focuses on the mouth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Pulpit: the fool meddles in quarrels that aren't his and makes them worse. Luke 21:35 uses the same Greek word for "snare." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: the KJV's "wounds" is better translated "dainty morsels," things swallowed eagerly. Perhaps it also hints that they are poisoned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html
- Guzik, quoting Waltke: unlike a fool's words that mainly harm himself, the talebearer's words destroy the relationships of others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/

**v. 9**
- Guzik, following G. Campbell Morgan: there is no neutral ground, and laziness destroys too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Henry applies it to religion: being careless in prayer is close to not praying at all. Omissions of duty and in duty are as fatal to the soul as commissions of sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_018.cfm

**v. 10**
- Guzik: the Name is not a magic charm. It stands for God's character, so you take refuge in each of his attributes. It is the only place in Proverbs where "the name of the LORD" appears (Ross). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Henry: the Name covers God's titles and attributes, and also his covenant and its promises. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_018.cfm
- Pulpit (Anglican) adds a sacramental note: Christians are baptized into this Name. It links the verse to Acts 4:12. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew for "imagination" means a picture. The rich man's security is only imagined. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html
- Guzik, quoting Garrett: wealth does protect somewhat, but it gives a false sense of more security than it can deliver. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/

**v. 12**
- Pride leads to destruction (cross-reference Proverbs 16:18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Pulpit: almost the same sayings appear in 16:18 and 15:33. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**v. 13**
- Pulpit gives parallels from Ecclesiasticus 11:8 and the Talmud. Its sermon notes call answering too early ungenerous and untruthful. The verdict should never go beyond the evidence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: the human spirit can hold the body up, but a broken spirit has nothing higher to lean on. Understood at its highest, the "spirit" points to God's grace strengthening a person. The Hebrew word for spirit changes gender between the two lines, which Pulpit takes as a sign of weakening. The LXX and Vulgate read the verse very differently. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html
- Henry applies it to a troubled conscience, so keep your conscience clear. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_018.cfm
- Guzik: when the spirit is broken, the will to live itself may be gone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/

**v. 15**
- Ross, quoted by Guzik: the ear listens and the heart discerns, which together means gaining knowledge fully. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/

**v. 16** (readings really differ)
- Guzik: this is a different word from the "bribe" in 17:8. Generosity and courtesy simply open doors. No gift is needed to come to Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Pulpit: not a bribe. It means a polite gift, like the Magi's. It rejects Hitzig's "spiritual gift" reading because the word never means that elsewhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html
- Clarke (Methodist) calls the custom a base and degrading practice. Barnes reads it as a bribe acting as a "friend at court." Constable, citing Waltke, thinks it fair to apply the verse to one's personal abilities (gifts) that he or she uses in the service of others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/18-16.html
- The Bible Hub study note applies it to God-given abilities and spiritual gifts. It adds that using a gift to gain access without integrity is condemned. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/18-16.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: "one story is good till the other is told." The Vulgate and LXX read it as "the righteous man accuses himself first," and Gregory the Great used that reading for confessing sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: the lot settled cases where the evidence conflicted, because it was considered to show the judgment of God. Without it, powerful men would settle disputes by violence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html
- Guzik, quoting Garrett: casting lots handed the dispute over to God. The principle extends to any agreed outside authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/

**v. 19**
- Pulpit: a close friend who has been wronged becomes an enemy who can't be reconciled. The context is still lawsuits. The LXX and Vulgate read the opposite, "a brother helped by a brother is like a strong city." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-18.html
- Guzik: avoid offending, and if offence comes, make sure the fault isn't yours. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/

**v. 20**
- Guzik, in his note on v. 21: this verse shows how a man's speech can feed his stomach. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Sam Storms (charismatic-Reformed) treats vv. 20–21 together. Our words can be a great blessing or a deadly weapon. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/your-words-have-the-power-of-life-and-death---proverbs-1820-21

**v. 21** (the debated modern teaching)
- Older writers: Gill applies it to witnesses, judges and preachers, and links it to Matthew 12:37. Clarke applies it especially to public pleaders, meaning advocates in court. Constable: This proverb is a warning to the talkative. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/18-21.html
- Pulpit: the Hebrew is literally "in the hand of the tongue," and speech pictures the mind. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/18-21.htm
- Lucky Mogakane (The Gospel Coalition Africa) answers the idea that Christians can "speak things into existence." He says he once held that view himself. The life and death language is hyperbolic, the verse is a warning about careless speech, and Only God can speak things into existence. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/can-we-speak-things-into-existence-considering-proverbs-1821/
- GotQuestions reads it in physical, spiritual and emotional terms. For example, a judge's word can decide whether someone lives. https://www.gotquestions.org/power-of-the-tongue.html

**v. 22** (traditions differ)
- Clarke (Methodist) takes the bare Hebrew as it stands: there are few cases where a wife of any sort is not better than none, because celibacy is an evil. He notes the ancient versions add "good."
- Constable: Not just any wife is a good thing though; only a good wife is. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/18-22.html
- Gill (Baptist) and Pulpit (Anglican) both say a good wife is meant. Barnes thinks the writer sees God joining every true marriage. The LXX and Vulgate add a line: whoever puts away a good wife puts away a good thing, and whoever keeps an adulteress is a fool. Pulpit thinks this reflects divorce practice at the time the LXX was made. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/18-22.htm
- GotQuestions notes the wording echoes 8:35, so after wisdom itself a good wife is God's best blessing. It stresses that proverbs are not guarantees. https://www.gotquestions.org/he-who-finds-a-wife.html

**v. 23**
- Only the Bible Hub chapter summary: need speaks softly, while wealth often answers harshly. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/proverbs/18.htm

**v. 24** (does it point to Christ?)
- The KJV's "must shew himself friendly" is widely rejected. Ellicott says the man of many friends wears himself out on hospitality and is deserted in trouble. Pulpit calls the KJV certainly not correct. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/18-24.htm
- Reads it as Christ: Spurgeon (Baptist): this friend is the blessed Redeemer, Jesus Christ. Henry and Chuck Smith say the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/18-24.html
- Against: Clarke (Methodist) says those who apply it to God or Christ are wrong, because the text has no such meaning. Constable sits in the middle: applying it to Christ is fine, but Solomon meant faithful human friends. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/18-24.html
- Guzik both applies it to Jesus and admits it is likely that Solomon did not have the Messiah in mind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-18/
- Sam Storms: keep your close friends few. The Hebrew for "sticks closer" means to cling and never betray. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/sticky-friends--proverbs-1824
